prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "S&P Global Inc." (ticker SPGI), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "SPGI", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: S&P Global Inc.
result.industry: Credit ratings, financial indices and market data
markets: Financial data, analytics and research desktops (Capital IQ Pro)
Stock market indices and index licensing (S&P 500, Dow Jones)
Commodity and energy price benchmarks and insights (Platts)
AI-ready data feeds and workflow tools (Kensho)

mission.source: Company website (Who We Are / Our Company page: "At S&P Global, we focus on Advancing Essential Intelligence.")
mission.plain: Give companies, investors and governments the trusted facts and scores they need to make big money decisions.

about.plain: S&P Global gives grades to companies and governments that borrow money, so lenders know how safe a loan is. It runs famous stock market scoreboards like the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average, and fund companies pay to use them. It also sells data, news and price benchmarks for oil, gas and metals, plus software that bankers and investors use to research companies.
about.customers: Banks, investment funds, companies that borrow money, governments, and energy and commodity traders.
about.everyday: The S&P 500 index that many people's retirement funds and index funds track is run by S&P Global's index business.

money.part: Market data and research software (Market Intelligence)
money.plain: Capital IQ Pro desktop, company data feeds and analytics subscriptions
Fees from borrowers to grade their bonds and loans
Benchmark prices, news and forecasts for oil, gas, power and metals
Licence fees for the S&P 500 and other indices, often a cut of ETF assets
Data on private funds and investors, bought for $1.8 billion in November 2025
Data delivered into AI assistants and workflows through Kensho APIs and connectors

result.summary: S&P Global has one of the widest moats in finance: it is one of three firms that dominate credit ratings, it owns the S&P 500 and Dow Jones index brands, and its Platts prices are written into commodity contracts. These are benchmarks that customers, regulators and contracts rely on, so they are very hard to replace, and they earn operating margins of about 64% (Ratings) and 69% (Indices) in 2025. Its weaker spot is the Market Intelligence data business, where Bloomberg, LSEG, FactSet and new AI tools compete harder.

pricingPower.evidence: Revenue rose every year from 2019's $6,699 million to $15,336 million in 2025 while GAAP operating profit reached $6,478 million (42.2% margin, 50.4% adjusted); Ratings earned a 63.8% segment margin and Indices 68.7% in 2025, and in Q2 2026 Ratings revenue grew 17% and Indices 20% with net renewal rates reported up 100 basis points, signs that price rises stick without losing customers.

moats.evidence: The S&P 500, Dow Jones Industrial Average, an S&P credit rating and a Platts price are household or industry-standard brands; S&P held 49.96% of all NRSRO ratings outstanding at end-2023 per the SEC.

Issuers need an S&P rating for bond investors and index mandates, ETF and fund products are written around S&P index methodologies, and Platts assessments are embedded in physical and derivative commodity contracts, so changing provider is costly and slow.

The more investors use S&P ratings and indices as the reference, the more issuers and fund sponsors must use them too, a two-sided benchmark effect that keeps the big three agencies at about 92% of NRSRO revenue.

With $15.3 billion of 2025 revenue and data spread across Ratings, Market Intelligence, Energy and Indices, it can spread data collection and technology costs over far more customers than smaller rivals.
Ratings is a regulated oligopoly where S&P, Moody's and Fitch hold about 94% of ratings outstanding; a new entrant would struggle to earn the investor trust that justifies the cost.
Its business model is the incumbent one; AI-native research tools and low-cost index providers are more likely to counter-position against it than the reverse.
Over 160 years of rating methodologies, historical default studies and index governance (the S&P 500 committee) are hard to copy quickly.
It exclusively owns the S&P 500 and Dow Jones index intellectual property (through S&P Dow Jones Indices, jointly owned with CME Group) and decades of proprietary ratings and company data.

customers.evidence: Most revenue is recurring subscriptions or asset-linked fees, management cited net renewal rates up 100 basis points in mid-2026, and Q2 2026 pro forma organic revenue grew 11%; customers have little alternative for a required rating or a contracted benchmark, though some resent rating fees.

talent.evidence: It employs 30,000+ people and is a well-regarded finance employer with a strong brand, but it is not usually near the top of broad best-places-to-work rankings and competes for data and AI engineers with Big Tech and Bloomberg.

product.evidence: S&P ratings and the S&P 500 are the reference products in their markets and Platts is a leading oil price benchmark; Capital IQ Pro is a solid second-tier desktop behind the Bloomberg Terminal, and API calls through its AI connectors were reported up 500% quarter-over-quarter in June 2026.

estimates.name: London Stock Exchange Group (FTSE Russell, LSEG Data & Analytics)

marketShare.market: NRSRO credit ratings outstanding (all categories, SEC Office of Credit Ratings)

threats: AI-native research tools and large language models could make desktop data products such as Capital IQ Pro (cited at under 6% of revenue) less necessary and pressure Market Intelligence pricing
Ratings revenue depends on bond issuance, which can drop sharply in credit downturns or high-rate periods
Regulatory and legal risk for rating agencies (conflict-of-interest scrutiny of the issuer-pays model, fines, EU and US rules)
Fee pressure on index licensing as low-cost ETFs push down basis-point fees and fund sponsors self-index
Competition from Bloomberg, LSEG, MSCI, Moody's and private-markets data firms such as PitchBook
Integration and capital-allocation risk from acquisitions (IHS Markit in 2022, With Intelligence in 2025) and a debt load larger than cash

ceo.name: Martina Cheung
ceo.background: Bachelor of Commerce and Master of Business Studies, National University of Ireland Galway; ex-Accenture strategy and Mitchell Madison partner; joined S&P in 2010 and ran Market Intelligence and Ratings

c1.evidence: S&P Global leads credit ratings and index licensing, but these are mature industries, not emerging ones; company revenue grew 7.9% in 2025 and 2026 guidance is 6-8% organic growth.

c2.evidence: Customers choose S&P because its ratings and the S&P 500 are the benchmarks investors, regulators and contracts require, an advantage built over more than a century that keeps the big three agencies at about 94% of ratings outstanding.

c3.evidence: Ordinary people recognise the S&P 500 and the Dow, and S&P is the default leader in ratings, but few know S&P Global the company or use its products directly.

c4.evidence: Its purpose 'Advancing Essential Intelligence' is used consistently, but it is a corporate statement rather than a deeply inspiring cause, and management is focused on margins and buybacks; better market transparency over 10 years would matter mainly to finance professionals.

c6.evidence: “trusted, benchmark, Wall Street, ratings agency”: investors see it as a high-quality compounder, while the public impression is neutral to mixed because rating agencies were blamed for the 2008 mortgage crisis.

c7.evidence: Its markets are large and growing with global debt, passive investing and private markets, but growth is mid-to-high single digit (2026 guidance 6-8% organic), not a CRWD- or NVDA-style secular surge.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into private markets data (With Intelligence, $1.8 billion, 2025), private credit ratings and AI data delivery through Kensho, but these extend existing franchises rather than open huge new markets.

m1.evidence: Martina Cheung has set a clear plan to focus on benchmarks and AI-ready data, spinning off Mobility on July 1, 2026, but she is a disciplined operator rather than a visionary in the founder mould.

m2.evidence: Cheung is a professional manager who joined in 2010 and became CEO on November 1, 2024; she is not a founder and the company is run in a conventional corporate way.

m4.evidence: There is no clear public evidence either way on a servant-leadership style beyond standard corporate statements about employees and customers.

m5.evidence: The company stresses AI integration (Kensho, AI connectors with API calls reported up 500% quarter-over-quarter in 2026), but its culture is known for rigour and integrity more than constant product invention.

m6.evidence: Cheung has a commerce and business studies background and a consulting and operations career, not an engineering one.

m7.evidence: There are no public controversies about her character, but nothing distinctive shows stewardship aimed beyond running a well-governed, profitable company.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Martina Cheung at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Cheung keeps a low, professional public profile rather than a distinctive celebrity personality.

m9.evidence: As head of Ratings she grew it to $3.3 billion of 2023 revenue at a 56.5% margin, and as CEO she delivered 2025 adjusted EPS of $17.83 (up 14%) and completed the Mobility spin-off on schedule.

m10.evidence: It is known for cost discipline and margin expansion (adjusted operating margin 50.4% in 2025, up 140 basis points) rather than for notable frugality symbols.

c10.evidence: Its ratings and indices make global capital markets work more cheaply, indirectly helping savers through low-cost S&P 500 index funds, but it does not touch people's lives directly the way Netflix or Google do.

p2.evidence: Building trusted ratings, index and price benchmarks is very hard to replicate and important for markets, though the underlying work is analysis and data rather than frontier technology.

f2.evidence: GAAP operating margin fell from 48.6% in 2020 and 50.9% in 2021 to 42.2% in 2025, mainly because of IHS Markit merger amortization ($1,069 million in 2025), though it has risen each year since 2023's 32.2%.

f3.evidence: Total debt of $15,170 million at June 30, 2026 exceeds cash of $4,134 million, but it is about 2.7 times 2025 operating cash flow of $5,651 million, equity is a positive $31.6 billion and interest is covered about 22 times.

f4.evidence: Operating profit rose from $3,617 million in 2020 to $6,478 million in 2025 and operating cash flow from $3,567 million to $5,651 million, though both dipped in 2022-2023 around the IHS Markit merger.

v1.evidence: In ratings and indices it is the default choice because investors and contracts ask for S&P, but in market data the Bloomberg Terminal is widely seen as the better product.

v2.evidence: No top-tier placement in major best-employer rankings was verified; it is seen as a solid, reputable finance employer.

c5.evidence: If it vanished, bond issuers, banks, fund managers and index funds tracking the S&P 500, plus oil and metals traders pricing contracts off Platts, would immediately lose benchmarks they depend on.
